title: Algebraic description of complex conjugation on cohomology of a smooth projective hypersurface

predicted_errors.error_location: Formula for μ (period ratio) appearing near Example 2.4/2.8: 'μ := (∫_{γ1}ω·∫_{γ2}ω − ∫_{γ2}ω·∫_{γ1}ω)/(24π√−1)'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: As written, the numerator ∫_{γ1}ω·∫_{γ2}ω − ∫_{γ2}ω·∫_{γ1}ω is the difference of two identical complex-number products (multiplication of complex numbers is commutative), so the expression is identically zero regardless of ω. This cannot be the intended quantity, since Example 2.8 uses this same μ as a nonzero transcendental coefficient (μ·yD(x)) that is essential to describing the real Hodge structure of the elliptic curve. By analogy with the analogous construction in Definition 2.2 (U_{k,γ}), the second factor in one of the two terms should involve the complex conjugate of a period integral (e.g. ∫_{γ1}ω·conj(∫_{γ2}ω) − ∫_{γ2}ω·conj(∫_{γ1}ω)), not the unconjugated period again. As stated, the formula is mathematically vacuous (≡0), contradicting its use elsewhere in the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Definition of μ in Section 2.2 ('Let μ be the C-dimension of H^{n-1}_prim(X,C)') versus the later formula labeled 'μ' used in Example 2.4/2.8 as a period-ratio constant
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The symbol μ is first defined as the total complex dimension of primitive middle cohomology (used throughout Section 2.2, e.g. μ = (e-1)/e((e-1)^n+(-1)^{n+1}), and μ=2g for even n). Later, in the material associated with Example 2.4/2.8, the same symbol μ is reused for an unrelated transcendental quantity defined via a period integral ('μ := (∫_{γ1}ω·∫_{γ2}ω − ∫_{γ2}ω·∫_{γ1}ω)/(24π√−1)'), which is then used as a scalar coefficient (μ·yD(x)) in Example 2.8. This dual use of the same symbol for two conceptually and dimensionally distinct objects (an integer Betti number vs. a complex period ratio) creates a direct textual inconsistency that would confuse readers and requires correction/renaming.
